title: Setting your hourly rate and minimum charge for Specialty appliance and machine cleaning
audience: Owners of small Australian property trade businesses who need a base rate and a minimum charge before quoting
learningOutcomes: Separate billable hours from non-billable hours, and calculate the time available to bill.
Calculate a base hourly rate from the owner's own costs and income target, then compare it with local evidence.
Set a minimum charge for short jobs, and explain it to a client before the visit.

instruction.heading: Factors that move the rate
instruction.body: A specialist appliance rate depends on the appliances you are trained to clean, the time each type takes, the equipment you carry, and the cost of running the business. A cleaner who can deliver several appliance types in one visit may justify a higher rate than one who cleans only ovens. Do not cut the rate to win work. The research found one Sydney vendor's list with per-appliance prices for ovens, cooktops and range hoods, and none for washing machines, dishwashers or fridges. Compare your own quotes against that list only as a sense check, and set rates for uncovered appliances from your own costs.

instruction.heading: Counting the hours that can be billed
instruction.body: Owners often price as though every hour of the week can be billed. Few can. Travel between visits, quoting, admin, marketing, equipment upkeep, sick days and leave are not billable. Estimate the paid working hours in a year, subtract the non-billable time, and you have billable hours. Jobber's guide puts billable time at about 60 to 80 percent of working hours, a general range rather than an Australian figure (Jobber, 5 November 2024, modified 20 July 2026). A mobile cleaner with several short visits in a day may sit at the lower end, so log one month before you rely on the range.

instruction.heading: Building the rate from costs and income
instruction.body: Add the annual costs of running the business, including insurance, registration, equipment and its upkeep, the vehicle, phone, software, marketing and accounting, to the income you need. A business.gov.au pricing guide says on-costs such as superannuation, leave and tax belong in the hourly figure, so decide how each applies to you (business.gov.au, 1 October 2026). Have a registered tax agent confirm how leave and superannuation are treated in your situation before the rate is published. Divide the total by billable hours to reach the base rate. A personal-training guide from AIPT works backwards from a target income, dividing by working weeks and then by weekly hours, with tax and business costs added on top (AIPT, 16 May 2025). Review the base rate each quarter.

instruction.heading: Setting a minimum charge for short visits
instruction.body: A short visit to clean one appliance can cost more in time than it earns, because travel, set-up and admin do not shrink with the job. A minimum charge covers the time to attend and start work. The Sydney vendor list sets a minimum for the service of $204 for non-members and $164 for Club members, above some single-item prices (Fantastic Cleaners, updated 15 July 2026). Contractor+ suggests setting a minimum from the full cost of the visit, divided by one minus the target margin, with the minimum covering travel, set-up and clean-up. Its figures are labelled illustrative and are not used here (Contractor+, 23 September 2026). Set your own minimum from your visit cost, and state it before the booking.

instruction.heading: Price one visit as one labour amount
instruction.body: A client who books an oven and a range hood in one visit should get one labour amount for the visit, not a separate minimum for each item. Contractor+ describes pricing several small tasks in one visit as one labour amount (Contractor+, 23 September 2026). Show each item on the quote so the client can see what is included, and price any extra work before you start it.

procedure: Estimate the paid working hours in a year, then subtract travel, admin, marketing, training, equipment upkeep and leave to find billable hours.
List the annual running costs, including insurance, registration, equipment, vehicle, phone, software and marketing.
Add the income needed, including allowances for leave and tax confirmed by a registered tax agent.
Divide the total by billable hours to find the base rate.
Set a minimum charge that covers travel, set-up and admin for a short visit, and state it in writing.
Review the rate each quarter, and record any change and the reason for it.

workedExamples.situation: An owner's calculation shows that only sixty of every hundred paid hours can be billed, but the owner plans to set the rate as if every paid hour could be billed.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What is the effect on the rate if the wrong assumption is kept?
workedExamples.reasoning: Pricing as if every paid hour were billable understates the rate, because the costs and the income still have to come out of the hours that can be billed. With sixty billable hours in every hundred, the costs of all one hundred paid hours must come from the sixty, so the rate needs to be about 1.67 times the rate for a fully billable week. The rate is built from billable hours, then checked against your own visit costs and the minimum charge before it is published.

workedExamples.situation: Illustrative: a client wants a single cooktop cleaned. The visit takes 0.5 hours on site and 40 minutes of travel. The Sydney vendor list shows a cooktop of up to four burners at $20 for a member and $60 for a non-member (Fantastic Cleaners, updated 15 July 2026).
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Should the hourly rate alone price this visit?
workedExamples.reasoning: No. An hourly rate applied to the 30 minutes on site leaves the 40 minutes of travel unpaid, so the effective rate for the visit is lower than the quoted one. The item price on the vendor list is a sense check, not the cost of the visit. A minimum charge that covers travel, set-up and admin is the better answer, and it is stated before the booking.

equipmentAndPpe: Log of paid and billable hours for one month, with travel recorded separately
Price sheet with the base rate, the minimum charge and the review date

commonErrors.error: Setting a rate from a published price list or a competitor's figure without checking your own costs. Gap: no sourced rate for washing machines, dishwashers or fridges.
commonErrors.prevention: Build the base rate from your own costs and billable hours, then compare it with your quotes and the local evidence you can verify.

commonErrors.error: Pricing as though every paid hour could be billed.
commonErrors.prevention: Subtract the non-billable time before dividing.

commonErrors.error: Taking short visits at the same rate, without covering travel and set-up.
commonErrors.prevention: Set and state a minimum charge that covers travel, set-up and admin.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Price display rules come from the Australian Consumer Law, as summarised in the ACCC price display guidance (2 October 2026). That guidance says the total must include unavoidable fees. It does not settle whether a minimum or call-out charge is a fair term. Check that point with current ACCC guidance or a legal adviser before publishing a price sheet.
Confirm how leave, superannuation and tax apply to your business with a registered tax agent. This lesson gives no tax advice.

qualityStandard: Billable hours are calculated from a logged or estimated month, not assumed.
The base rate is built from the owner's costs and income target, and is compared with local evidence.
A minimum charge is set and stated before any short visit.
documentationEvidence: Annual costs and income worksheet, with the source and date of each cost
Billable hours calculation showing the non-billable deductions
Price sheet showing the base rate, the minimum charge and the review date
summary: Price from billable hours, not from paid hours.
Build the rate from costs and a stated income target, then check it against your own visits and verified local evidence.
Set and state a minimum charge for short visits. Gap: no sourced minimum for appliance work outside one Sydney vendor list.

knowledgeChecks.question: A cleaner can bill only some of the paid hours. How should the rate be built?
options: From all paid hours, so the rate looks lower and the client pays less per visit
From billable hours, so the costs and income are covered by the work that can be billed
From the average on a vendor's price list and the rate listed by the nearest competitor
From the rate the owner wishes the market would pay

knowledgeChecks.question: Why set a minimum charge for a short appliance visit?
options: Because a short visit needs travel but no set-up time at all
Because travel, set-up and admin time does not shrink with the size of the visit
Because clients expect every visit to cost the same amount
Because a minimum charge replaces a written quote

knowledgeChecks.question: What is the best source for checking a base hourly rate for appliance cleaning?
options: A single published national average from another trade
Your own costs and billable hours, compared with verifiable local evidence
A friend's rate, without checking the costs or the local market
The first price shown on a bidding site this week

officialReferences.title: Price displays (ACCC)
officialReferences.covers: States that the total price must include unavoidable fees, shown as a single figure. Does not address minimum or call-out charges, or tax on leave and superannuation, which remain unconfirmed. Publisher: ACCC.
